description: How Englishness and Britishness have been defined, contested and reimagined across a thousand years.
content_html:
The Constructed Nature of British Identity

One of the most important arguments in migration history is that national identity is not fixed or primordial — it is historically constructed. “Englishness” and “Britishness” have meant different things in different centuries, and what has been considered authentically “British” has constantly been redrawn in response to migration, empire, war and political change. Recognising this is essential to understanding why migration has been so contentious — because it always involves questions about who belongs.

Historian Linda Colley argued in her 1992 book Britons that British national identity was “forged” rather than found — created during the eighteenth century through shared Protestantism, war with France, and the experience of building an empire. Before the Act of Union of 1707, “Britain” barely existed as a meaningful identity. English, Scots, Welsh and Irish had distinct identities. The creation of “Britishness” was a deliberate political project, not the expression of a pre-existing ethnic unity.

Key Fact

The Act of Union of 1707 united England and Scotland politically. Scotland retained its own legal and church systems but shared a Parliament at Westminster. The Union was contested in Scotland from the start — there were Jacobite risings in 1715 and 1745. But over the eighteenth century, Scottish elites increasingly participated in the British Empire as merchants, soldiers and administrators, and “Britishness” became a meaningful identity alongside Scottish identity. Irish union followed in 1801, though it was always more contested.

Britishness and Empire

The British Empire was central to how “Britishness” was understood from the eighteenth to the mid-twentieth century. Empire gave meaning to British identity by defining it against “the other” — the colonised peoples of Africa, Asia and the Americas. The 1948 British Nationality Act’s inclusion of all Commonwealth subjects as British citizens was, in part, a final expression of this imperial identity — the idea that Britons were spread across the globe and were all subjects of the same Crown.

But the arrival of Caribbean and South Asian migrants in the 1950s revealed the contradiction at the heart of imperial Britishness: people who were legally British, who had often served Britain in the Second World War, found that “Britishness” in practice was racialised. The hostility of the 1958 riots, the “No Coloured” signs in lodging houses, and Enoch Powell’s 1968 speech all expressed an idea of Britishness that was ethnically exclusive, despite the legal reality of Commonwealth citizenship.

Diaspora identity became a key concept for understanding the experience of migrant communities in late-twentieth-century Britain. Stuart Hall argued that Black British identity was not simply “Caribbean” transplanted to Britain, nor simply “British” in the traditional sense, but something new — a hybrid, evolving identity shaped by the experience of migration and the encounter with British culture. This challenged both those who argued migrants should “go back” and those who demanded complete assimilation into a homogeneous British culture.

Hall’s ideas influenced how policymakers, educators and cultural institutions thought about diversity. The multicultural model of the 1990s — expressed in the Parekh Report — drew on this intellectual tradition. It argued that a diverse society could be cohesive without requiring everyone to abandon their distinct cultural inheritance.

Devolution and the Fragmentation of Britishness

In 1997, referendums in Scotland and Wales produced majorities in favour of devolved legislatures. The Scottish Parliament and National Assembly for Wales opened in 1999. Devolution fundamentally changed the political geography of Britain: Scotland now had its own parliament with tax-varying powers; Wales had an assembly with secondary legislative powers. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 established a power-sharing executive in Northern Ireland. Together these changes reflected a growing sense that “Britishness” was compatible with multiple national identities — one could be Scottish and British, Welsh and British, or Northern Irish and British (or Northern Irish and Irish).

The Scottish independence referendum of 2014 put this to the test. In a high-turnout vote, 55% voted to remain in the United Kingdom; 45% voted for independence. The result was clear but the question was not settled: the Scottish National Party continued to campaign for independence, particularly after the Brexit vote of 2016 (which Scotland voted against). Whether devolution ultimately strengthened or weakened British identity remains a live question.

Key Fact

The Life in the UK test, introduced in 2002, attempted to define Britishness through a formal citizenship process. Applicants had to demonstrate knowledge of British history, institutions and civic values. The test represented a move towards a civic model of Britishness — membership defined by knowledge and commitment, not by ethnic origin. Critics noted that many long-term British residents would fail the test, suggesting that it measured a particular version of Britishness rather than the lived reality of belonging.

The tension between assimilation and integration runs through the entire thousand-year sweep of this thematic study. Norman migrants assimilated rapidly within two or three generations, with French and English eventually merging into Middle English. Huguenot refugees anglicised their names and merged into Protestant English society within two generations. But other communities — medieval Jews before 1290, the post-Windrush Caribbean community — maintained distinct identities precisely because they were excluded from full assimilation by the hostility of the host society.

Roy Jenkins’s 1966 definition of integration as “not a flattening process of assimilation but equal opportunity accompanied by cultural diversity in an atmosphere of mutual tolerance” remains the most influential attempt in British political history to define how a diverse society should work. Whether that vision has been achieved — and what obstacles have stood in its way — is the central evaluative question for this thematic study.
exam_tip_html: This final lesson is partly historiographical — it is about how historians and policymakers have understood British identity. For “Change and Continuity” essays, use Linda Colley’s argument that Britishness was ‘forged’ rather than natural as a framing point. The contrast between assimilation (demanded of many migrants) and integration (Roy Jenkins’s model) is a useful analytical tool for any question about the reception of migrants. Always name Stuart Hall or Bhikhu Parekh when discussing multiculturalism — they represent the intellectual tradition that the Parekh Report drew on.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Historian Linda Colley argued that “Britishness” was “forged” in the eighteenth century through Protestantism, war with France and Empire — it was not an ancient ethnic inheritance but a historically constructed identity, shaped by and continuously reshaped by migration.
  • Stuart Hall’s concept of diaspora identity challenges both assimilation and cultural separation, arguing that Black British identity is a hybrid, evolving form that reflects the encounter between migrant and host culture — an insight that underpins the multicultural model expressed in the Parekh Report (2000).
  • Devolution (1999) and the Scottish independence referendum (2014) reflect the ongoing fragmentation and renegotiation of Britishness, while the Life in the UK test (2002) represents one attempt to define civic Britishness — both show that questions of identity, belonging and migration remain as contested at the end of this thematic study as they were at its beginning.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Linda Colley's argument about the origins of British identity.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Colley argued that British identity was 'forged' rather than natural (1); she dated the creation of Britishness to the eighteenth century, driven by shared Protestantism and war with France (1). Feature 2: Colley argued that before the Act of Union of 1707, 'Britain' barely existed as a meaningful identity (1); English, Scots, Welsh and Irish had separate identities, and Britishness was a political construction built on top of these (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why the meaning of 'Britishness' changed significantly between 1948 and 1981.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons developed with evidence. Reason 1: The 1948 British Nationality Act defined Britishness broadly to include all Commonwealth subjects, expressing an imperial vision of a global British community; by 1981, this vision had been abandoned and the Act divided nationality into tiers based on ancestral connection to the UK. Reason 2: The arrival of Caribbean and South Asian migrants revealed that practical 'Britishness' was racialised — legal citizenship did not mean social acceptance; the hostility migrants faced showed that many people defined British identity in ethnic rather than civic terms. Secure: Both with evidence. Developing: One explained. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Stuart Hall argued that Black British identity was a 'hybrid' rather than simply Caribbean or simply British.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Hall's argument that diaspora identities are formed through the encounter between the migrant's cultural heritage and the culture of the host society; neither the original culture nor simple assimilation captures the lived experience; Black British culture created new forms (music, fashion, language, art) that drew on both traditions. Connects this to the political context of the 1970s-80s when Black British people faced racism and needed a positive identity that was neither rejection of Britishness nor denial of Caribbean heritage. Secure: Explains the hybrid concept with evidence. Developing: Describes Hall's ideas without full explanation. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which devolution changed the meaning of 'Britishness' after 1999.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Examples: devolution showed that Britishness was compatible with distinct national identities — one could be Scottish and British (1), as Scotland retained its own legal and educational system alongside Westminster membership (1); devolution created political institutions that expressed specifically Scottish and Welsh identities (1), meaning 'British' became a looser, multi-layered category than it had been under a unitary state (1). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that the history of migration to Britain shows that 'Britishness' has always been defined by exclusion rather than inclusion? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument that identifies both exclusion (Edict of Expulsion 1290 targeting Jews; Aliens Act 1905; 1962 and 1968 Commonwealth Immigrants Acts; 1981 Nationality Act; 1919 race riots) and inclusion (Huguenot naturalisation; Polish Resettlement Act; 1948 Act's broad citizenship; Race Relations Acts; Parekh Report's civic model). Argues that the balance between exclusion and inclusion has shifted over time and has never been uniform — reception depended on race, religion, economic context and political circumstance. Engages with Linda Colley, Stuart Hall or Bhikhu Parekh. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across multiple periods. Developing: Some comparative points with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the idea of 'integration' (as defined by Roy Jenkins) differed from the idea of 'assimilation'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two differences explained causally. Difference 1: Assimilation required migrants to abandon their distinct cultural identity and adopt the majority culture; Jenkins's integration model preserved cultural diversity alongside civic participation. Difference 2: Assimilation assumed a single dominant culture that migrants must conform to; integration assumed a shared civic framework (equal opportunity, democratic values) within which multiple cultures could coexist — this underpinned the Parekh Report's 'community of communities' model. Secure: Two differences explained. Developing: One difference explained. Emerging: General statements.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Linda Colley's main argument about British identity?
flashcard_questions.a: Britishness was 'forged' in the eighteenth century through Protestantism, war with France and Empire — not an ancient ethnic inheritance

flashcard_questions.q: What was Linda Colley's book, and when was it published?
What did the Act of Union (1707) do?
flashcard_questions.a: United England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain
The identity of a community displaced from its homeland that maintains connections to it while building a new life elsewhere

flashcard_questions.q: What did Stuart Hall mean by 'hybrid' Black British identity?
flashcard_questions.a: Black British identity was shaped by both Caribbean heritage and British culture — neither simply transplanted nor assimilated

flashcard_questions.q: What did Roy Jenkins mean by 'integration'?
flashcard_questions.a: Not assimilation but equal opportunity with cultural diversity in an atmosphere of mutual tolerance

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Scottish Parliament and National Assembly for Wales open?
What was the result of the 2014 Scottish independence referendum?
flashcard_questions.a: 55% voted to remain in the UK; 45% voted for independence

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between assimilation and integration?
flashcard_questions.a: Assimilation demands abandoning cultural identity; integration allows cultural diversity within a shared civic framework

glossary_terms.definition: A view, associated with historians like Linda Colley, that national identities are shaped by historical circumstances, politics and shared experience, not by unchanging ethnic or cultural essence.

British historian whose 1992 book Britons: Forging the Nation 1707-1837 argued that British identity was created in the eighteenth century through Protestantism, war with France and Empire, rather than being an ancient ethnic inheritance.
The 1707 Act that united the Kingdom of England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain, creating a new political entity and, over time, a new shared identity.

The experience of a population that has been displaced from its original homeland, maintaining connections to that homeland while building a new life elsewhere — relevant to Jewish, Caribbean, South Asian and many other communities in Britain.
Jamaican-born cultural theorist (1932-2014) who developed influential theories about Black British identity as hybrid, changing and positioned between multiple cultural inheritances.

A 2002 test introduced by the British government requiring applicants for settlement or citizenship to demonstrate knowledge of British life, history and institutions as a condition of naturalisation.
The process by which migrants or minority communities give up their distinct cultural identity and adopt the culture of the majority society.
